transcript:
This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management, all in one place, no matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how. You can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston. The lawyer representing Jane Doe in the Cornell rape case says students at other schools are contacting him.
Thomas Jiffra says they've described sexual assaults they reported to their colleges. Some told him their complaints were never followed up on.
Speaking to CNN, Jiffra says those accounts point to a problem that extends beyond Cornell.
I've received many emails from students, not just at Cornell, at other schools saying that they were sexually assaulted on campus.
They made complaints and it wasn't followed up on. And that's the real scary part. This isn't just a Cornell problem. This is a college-wide problem.
I've heard from women as far back as 40 years ago saying they were raped in a fraternity house and not at Cornell, at different places. And I think that's the important part of this case is we're learning as a society that college sexual assault is a huge problem.
The president of Cornell University released a video message on Saturday pledging transparency as the investigation moves forward.
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito says he's considered retiring. NPR's Kerry Johnson reports on fresh interviews with the justice as he promotes his new book.
Justice Alito tells CBS News he's considered retiring from the court. Alito, who's 76 years old, was appointed by President George W. Bush.
He's already served 20 years on the Supreme Court and written major decisions reversing the right to abortion and pairing back the Voting Rights Act.
Any justice's decision to retire before 2028 could set off a political tug of war. Senate Republicans famously refused to even meet with President Obama's nominee, Merrick Garland, because they said it was too close to an election.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
A planned release of emergency oil reserves could help ease pressure on global diesel markets.
NPR's Julia Simon reports G7 leaders agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of oil and refined products over the next four months.
In recent weeks, diesel prices have reached record highs, pushed up by shortages and damage to refineries in the Middle East and Russia, as Ukrainian drone strikes continue to hit Russian refineries.
Last month, diesel topped $6.50 a gallon here in the U.S. For context, diesel was around $3.75 in September of last year. That's more than 70% lower.
Diesel prices are even higher in some European countries. Earlier, President Trump had threatened to cut off U.S. diesel exports, which both American oil companies and European leaders opposed.
Julia Simon, NPR News.
This is NPR. In Ethiopia, federal forces have entered the capital of the Tigray region after over a week of intense fighting. The Tigray People's Liberation Front has retreated from the city, as Emmett Livingstone reports.
Videos on social media showed truckloads of troops entering Michaelae, the capital of the Tigray region, waving Ethiopian flags. It's a huge setback for the Tigray People's Liberation Front, or TPLF, which launched what it called a defensive war against the federal government on September 23rd.
The two sides already fought a civil war between 2020 and 2022, estimated to have killed 600,000 people. Tensions were left to fester, then erupted into a new round of conflict last month. Amid intense fighting, pro-government forces captured strategic towns in the Tigray region this week.
They then announced they had captured Michaelae's airport, and on Sunday said they were already pushing north of the regional capital. The TPLF appears to have abandoned the city without a fight. For NPR News, I'm Emmett Livingstone.
The Supreme Court opens its new term tomorrow with a case that could shape whether communities can sue oil and gas companies over climate change. Officials in Boulder County, Colorado, want the companies to help pay for damage from disasters linked to a warming climate.
It's one of dozens of governments across the country bringing similar lawsuits with billions of dollars at stake. The energy companies argue that climate change is a global issue that should not be decided in state courts.
I'm Windsor Johnston, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Lawyer for Cornell rape case says students at other schools report similar unreported sexual assaults
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito says he has considered retiring from the court
G7 leaders agree to release 100 million barrels of oil to ease global diesel shortage
Ethiopian federal forces enter Tigray regional capital after intense fighting with TPLF forces
Supreme Court takes up case on whether communities can sue oil companies for climate damage
